articles.title: Australia crush New Zealand to win fourth Women’s Rugby League World Cup
articles.summary: Australia dominated the first half and capitalised on the Kiwi Ferns’ errors to win 34-10 and clinch the trophy.
articles.body:
Winger Jaime Chapman collected a hat-trick as Australia crushed New Zealand 34-10 on Sunday with an emphatic first-half performance to clinch their fourth consecutive Women’s Rugby League World Cup title.

Two tries in the opening five minutes did the damage, and there were four more before half-time to send the Jillaroos to the break with a commanding 34-6 advantage.

Despite applying pressure, they were unable to add to their score as the humid conditions in Brisbane took their toll and errors crept in.

But Australia had done enough to ensure a fourth straight title, beating the Kiwi Ferns in the final each time, to reinforce their status as the sport’s powerhouse nation.

“I want to thank the Kiwi Ferns. It’s been such a great rivalry for so many years now, with so much respect between the two of our teams,” said Australia captain Isabelle Kelly, now a three-time World Cup champion.

“To my team … I’m just so humbled and honoured to be able to lead you guys. This has definitely been a dream come true, and I knew that we could get the job done.”

Before Australia’s global rise, New Zealand won the World Cup in 2000, 2003 and 2008.

“We didn’t quite get the job done today, but we are going to assert dominance back into this jersey,” said New Zealand skipper Raecene McGregor.

“The best of the Kiwi Ferns is yet to be shown, so stay with us.”

New Zealand had won only one of their previous 12 Tests against the Jillaroos dating back to 2017, and they were under the pump immediately.

A knock-on near the New Zealand try line just two minutes in allowed Australia to spread the ball wide, and Chapman dived over in the corner for her 11th try of the tournament.

With all the momentum, Australia pressured New Zealand into another mistake and capitalised, with Shaylee Bent crashing over for their second converted try.

Midway through the first half, they were 18-0 ahead, with another Chapman special on the back of a lightning break.

A sensational solo effort from Jessica Sergis stretched the lead further, with the five-eighth shrugging off three tackles to sprint the length of the field.

New Zealand finally got on the board when Shannon Mato barged across, but Chapman’s third came after she burst through two tackles to race away, putting Australia back in full control before Tamika Upton added a sixth before half-time.

Australia started strongly in the second half with only some desperate Kiwi defence keeping them at bay.

But it was a much tighter affair, with New Zealand’s Mackenzie Wiki crossing in the dying seconds for the only try of the half.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Australia's Reece Walsh says: 'I feel we got disrespected'
articles.summary: Reece Walsh gave a powerful response to Australia's critics as they secured a fourth successive World Cup triumph, saying that: "I feel we got disrespected."
articles.body:
Another Rugby League World Cup, another Australia triumph.

On Sunday, the Kangaroos served up their best performance of the tournament when it mattered most to overpower New Zealand 32-12.

It ensured a fourth consecutive title and a 10th in the past 11 World Cups, stretching back to 1975.

And the manner of the victory prompted superstar full-back Reece Walsh to question the audacity of those in the media who had written them off.

The debate around the Australia pack has bubbled throughout the tournament - with forward Tino Fa'asuamaleaui and captain Isaah Yeo both dismissing suggestions that Kevin Walters' side have been overpowered at times.

Much of that stems from the opening match on 15 October, when New Zealand lost 24-22 when they could and perhaps should have won an epic contest, and the way in which Fiji got close 10 days later before going down 36-22.

Australia found a way in both of those matches - and as they prepared to lift the Paul Barriere Trophy for a record-extending 13th time, Walsh delivered his own less-than-diplomatic response to the topic.

"I'm pretty speechless to be honest," said Walsh.

"The chat from everybody coming into this tournament, everyone wrote us off, talking about how good all the other teams are and how good their coaches are.

"I feel we got disrespected. Seeing all the Aussie fans coming out - how's that for culture, baby? I am so happy for Kevvie and the coaching staff.

"It was tough there but we kept building each week, believing in each other. This is something I'm going to remember for such a long time."

Triumph or flop? The Rugby League World Cup that split opinion

Dominant Australia defeat New Zealand in Men's World Cup final

Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup

The sight of Walsh doubled up and vomiting was one of the most striking images of that opener against New Zealand a month ago, with the Brisbane Broncos number one clearly lacking fitness going into the World Cup after an eight-week lay off.

He acknowledges now that he was desperate to win a race against time and shrug off an ankle injury to contribute to the Kangaroos' success.

"I kept telling Kev [head coach Kevin Walters] it was sweet but I wasn't sweet," he said.

"It was hurting that first game. Coming off eight weeks of rehab, I was unfit, I didn't touch a ball but the belief Kev had in me, all the boys made my job so easy. To be out here now and win for Australia, I am so proud."

Walsh's presence meant that James Tedesco, who captained Australia to victory four years ago, mainly played a back-seat role at this World Cup.

But the 33-year-old Sydney Roosters full-back, who announced his international retirement immediately after the match, was unexpectedly thrown as mark of respect for his standing in the game.

Tedesco added the Clive Churchill medal to a stack of individual accolades in 2026 and has also won three NRL Premiership titles and two World Cups.

"Teddy has been such a great player for a long time. We can only have one full-back but James with his season, it was just reward," Walters added.

"He didn't tell me [he was retiring]. The reason James got on was because I respect him as a player and a person and what he has done for our game and as a former Australia captain.

"Without being disrespectful with the scoreline, I thought he needed to get on the field and experience that. I am so glad that happened now because he has been a champion in the jersey and the sport."

While Australia peaked at just the right time, New Zealand's levels dipped considerably in their first final since 2013, which meant a gripping and cloesly-fought encounter never materialised.

"Any time you get to a final and don't get the result it is always going to be a missed opportunity," said Kiwis head coach Stacey Jones.

"It was our worst performance. We got off to a bad start and could not fight our way out of it. When you make errors and your discipline is poor and give them all that ball, no matter what team you are it is just too hard."

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Defensive desire a Welsh hallmark - Jamie Roberts
articles.summary: Former Wales centre Jamie Roberts says the heroic defensive effort to beat New Zealand for the first time since 1953 showed what it meant to be Welsh.
articles.body:
Former British and Irish Lions centre Jamie Roberts said Wales' heroic defensive effort against New Zealand in the 35-28 win showed what it meant to be Welsh.

It was the first time since 1953 Wales celebrated beating the All Blacks, ending a run of 34 successive defeats in one of world rugby's historically most one-sided fixtures.

On three separate occasions Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defence that denied the visitors.

"That defensive set in the second half epitomised in a way what it is to be Welsh," Roberts, who won 94 caps for Wales, told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"That resilience, that bravery, that kind of never-say-die attitude that made us all so proud."

Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo

'One of the greatest wins' - Wales stun All Blacks to go from no-hopers to heroes

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

Wales made a massive 346 tackles, setting a new world record for Tests that outstripped the previous mark of 292 set last year by France in New Zealand.

Lock Dafydd Jenkins topped the charts at 38, which matches the individual world record tally set by France captain Thierry Dusautoir in the 2007 World Cup quarter-final at the same Cardiff ground.

Jenkins was followed by Jac Morgan (31), James Botham (30), centre Eddie James (25) and Dewi Lake (24).

Wales had the top nine tacklers on the field, with replacement prop Gareth Thomas making 19 in just 26 minutes.

"It's heroic and as the days go past we would just appreciate it a little bit more how special yesterday was," said Roberts.

"I woke up this morning just thinking had it happened?

"It was unbelievable and only sport can make you feel those emotions."

A generational victory after tough times

Roberts says he hopes the players understand the magnitude of the victory.

"It's a generational win and I salute the 23 lads who put in that heroic performance," said Roberts.

"I hope the lads appreciate what they've done for the country by putting a huge amount of pride in the jersey for a generational win.

"It's a young squad that's finding their way, we're developing combinations as we look ahead to the World Cup next year."

Roberts is also a Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) board member at a time when the game has been in disarray in Wales on and off the field.

The WRU board is proposing to cut a professional side by 2028 while the governing has posted an £18m loss .

The Wales men's national team slumped to a record 18 straight Test defeats in a winless run that lasted 16 months, which also saw the side slip to a lowest world ranking of 14th.

"Therein lies the the kind of David v Goliath narrative," said Roberts.

"You have to put this one in context of where Wales have been in the last couple of years.

"They've been in a very difficult place and that's what makes the win all the more sweet.

"It's a group of young men who have gone through a lot of challenges in the last couple of years and there lies the resilience, heart and effort.

"A lot of those players have gone through such a difficult time, so to come out swinging like that and perform like that was sensational."

Reality dawns after Wales dared to dream

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

'We've waited 73 years to be here' - Wales fans ecstatic after win over New Zealand

Achieving something that Welsh legends could not

This class of 2026 achieved something that Grand Slam-winning sides could not manage with legends such as Sir Gareth Edwards, who never beat the All Blacks with Wales, in the Cardiff crowd to witness the spectacular scenes.

"So many good and great Wales sides down the years have failed to beat the All Blacks at a time where they were higher ranked," said Roberts.

"Trophy-winning teams have failed to do it and that's what makes this win all the more remarkable and special."

Roberts says the pride was felt inside and outside of the Principality Stadium.

"I've not felt emotions like that in a long time, certainly not since I've retired, seeing how much happiness there was around the place was unbelievable," said Roberts.

"Not just the people at the stadium had a huge amount of awe in that performance, but it touched everyone watching around the world.

"There was so much joy out around Cardiffc, and that would be reflected across the country and for Welsh people across the globe."

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2026: Has tournament set a new benchmark for international rugby league?
articles.summary: Has the Rugby League World Cup set a new benchmark for the international game? BBC Sport discovers the answer to that question differs in the northern and southern hemispheres.
articles.body:
Has the 2026 Rugby League World Cup been a success or not?

It depends on who you listen to - and perhaps where in the world you are.

The men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments provided plenty of stories - from Kalyn Ponga's return from a broken arm in 23 days, to Jodie Cunningham's mangled ear, , external to the England wheelchair team's golden ladder, to the men's group format that caused widespread bafflement.

But was the World Cup a triumph? The northern and southern hemisphere perspectives provide contrasting answers.

For the fourth tournament running, Australia won the men's and women's titles, with New Zealand unable to deliver a twist in either final.

Tonga and Samoa brought vibrancy and passion - performing to a level that underlined why they are being elevated to Tier One status. The large Polynesian population in the USA - which will co-host the 2030 men's and women's World Cups - is likely to be key in spreading the rugby league word further around the world.

England's Wheelchair World Cup win, in a thunderous final against their old foes France, offset some of the disappointment felt when Brian McDermott's men and Stuart Barrow's women went home early.

And unlike when the game was emerging from post-pandemic constraints in 2022, the tournament has also worked financially by posting a profit.

"This whole tournament's been incredible," said Australia men's captain Isaah Yeo.

"Not just the fans here for New Zealand and Australia, but just everyone. I thought it was all outstanding.

"I think it's to date the most competitive and the best World Cup there's been. I think that's only going to continue to grow."

That sentiment has been endorsed repeatedly by Australian television broadcaster Channel Seven, which paid a reported A$12m (£6.1m) for exclusive domestic free-to-air coverage of the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.

Not everyone has been able to feel that positivity, though.

The decision to cut the men's tournament from 16 teams to 10 reduced the overall number of matches - and deprived teams such as Jamaica and Greece of a chance to build on the feelgood factor they provided as debutants in 2022.

That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.

For those who did get to the party this time, it has not always been an even contest. The disparity between the haves and have-nots has been significant.

While the Jillaroos and Kangaroos players will each receive equal payments of $40,000 (£20,500) for competing, Wales will reportedly spread a total of $15,000 (£7,689) across their women's and wheelchair teams. , external

Viewer access to the World Cup has varied too. While Australia had free-to-air live television coverage, fans in the UK only got it for the wheelchair final, shown on BBC iPlayer. For all other games, they needed a Premier Sports subscription, which was also the only way to watch the tournament in North America.

With many matches staged at times when British and American viewers were likely to be in bed, it feels as if a chance to spread the game's gospel has been missed.

Festival feel or competitive balance? Or neither?

Many of the players at this World Cup were Australia-based, as they play club rugby in either the NRL's men's competition or its Women's Premiership.

That helped the International Rugby League - the world governing body - to keep costs down, after it spent a vast sum transporting players from the southern hemisphere to England four years ago.

Paring back the men's competition also helped on the costs front, though another supposed benefit - cutting out the lopsided group-stage scorelines of four years ago - has not been evident.

France and the Cook Islands both conceded more than 180 points in the group stage, while scoring a combined 58.

Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live earlier this month that the men's World Cup had suffered for being slimmed down - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy and Wales also missing out.

"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.

"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.

"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.

"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."

A format that contained no quarter-finals came in for widespread criticism from pundits , external before a ball was kicked.

The men's tournament featured one group of four and another of six. But two teams went through from both groups, and not everyone in the six-team pool played each other.

In the words of Castleford Tigers head coach Paul Rowley, the former England hooker: "It's trying to make a square with five sides." England captain George Williams, during the build-up, called the format "weird".

And England turned out to be the major losers. The draw left them with no margin for error as an underprepared and jet-lagged squad faced a dangerous Tonga side first up, and lost 30-12.

And ultimately, McDermott's side paid the price. Of the 26 teams across the three World Cups, only one side won two out of three group games and still failed to make the semi-finals: England's men.

'We got disrespected' - Walsh and Australia make World Cup point

Ruthless Australia win record fourth Women's World Cup

Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won World Cup

An October and November tournament brings a different vibe depending on where you are. The last World Cup, in the UK, was staged as the temperatures dropped. This time around, it was held with co-hosts Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea heading towards summer.

Fans have gone to games in T-shirts and shorts instead of thick winter garments - and tellingly, average footfall increased.

That is despite the fact that the capacity 52,000 crowd in Brisbane for finals night was lower than the 67,000 at Old Trafford four years ago.

In 2022, the men's group stage - spanning 24 games - was watched by an average crowd of 9,811, itself down on the 14,345 figure from 2013, when England and Wales played hosts.

This time around, the average crowd rose to 21,360. It probably helped that there were fewer group games. It certainly helped that every Australia match was well attended, and that there was strong backing for New Zealand, Samoa, Tonga and Papua New Guinea, who played twice in their capital Port Moresby.

Lessons have also clearly been learned from 2022's heavily criticised ticket pricing structure.

Instead of adults paying more than £20 to attend matches, it has been a more friendly A$19, which equates to £9.74 per ticket.

But while attendances at this year's tournament are up, there is still work to be done around the women's game.

The sight of more empty seats than supporters in grounds for a number of double-headers is hardly a good look for the organisers or broadcasters.

Jillaroos coach Jess Skinner notably raised the issue after her team defeated Samoa 40-0 in their Pool A opener at the home of Parramatta Eels on 16 October.

That match had followed Samoa's men thrashing France 78-4 - but in a stadium with a capacity of 30,000, many of the recorded 13,174 crowd had dispersed before the women's game got under way, with the stands appearing barely 20% full.

"Let's get around women in sport, right? All women in sport, particularly at this Rugby League World Cup," Skinner said. "We've got a lot of talented women across all the teams and the message would be to stay and support that.

"Something really cool's happening in this generation of sport, with our ladies, and you're going to miss history-making moments at this World Cup, no doubt."

Sadly for Skinner and her peerless team, it was a pattern that was repeated in Sunday's final, with the stands in Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium only filling as kick-off time for the men's game approached.

Four years ago, the Rugby League World Cup was shown free-to-air in the UK by the BBC, with record-breaking viewing figures.

Almost 30 million people tuned in to watch the five-week extravaganza.

This time, the action has largely been behind a paywall. Premier Sports has shown all the World Cup matches live. The BBC showed the wheelchair final live, plus online highlights of selected games from all three tournaments.

In addition, it provided live radio coverage of all men's matches and some women's games, plus live text commentaries on selected games.

Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League - and not the Rugby Football League. Last month, IRL chair Troy Grant told the iPaper that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money - though no other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer either.

Former England international Jon Wilkin highlighted the issue during a BBC Radio 5 Live discussion at the start of this month, saying: "The World Cup should have been on the BBC.

"There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."

In response, a BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."

And therein lies a problem for the sport in the northern hemisphere, where more backing, more financial support and more coverage is needed to reverse the fortunes of the Super League and international teams largely bound to that competition.

The financial gulf to southern hemisphere's elite competitions was laid bare, when the NRL struck a record A$5.3bn (£2.78bn) television deal over seven years in July.

Super League's TV deal with Sky Sports, which expired at the end of 2026, was worth around £21.5m per year.

Even with the pending announcement of a deal to bring NRL investment into Super League, that particular playing field is a long way from being levelled.

And it means that when the next World Cup comes around, Australia can expect to be favourites to win the men's and women's tournaments again.

articles.title: Scotland 15-12 Australia - report
articles.summary: Scotland edge a dull Nations Championship encounter against Australia at Murrayfield.
articles.body:
Tries: M Fagerson, Dempsey Con: Russell Pens: Russell

Scotland edged a dull Nations Championship encounter against Australia at Murrayfield, a game that brought rugby fans crashing back down to earth after the brilliance of France's win against South Africa on Friday and the jaw-dropping wonder of Wales beating the All Blacks on Saturday.

Matt Fagerson, an impressive juggernaut, and Jack Dempsey scored for Scotland, Harry Potter got one for Australia, all in the first half hour.

We waited another 47 minutes before Finn Russell banged over a penalty to make it 15-5. Max Jorgensen's converted try with seconds remaining narrowed the gap. A little flurry at the end of a hugely disappointing, attritional Test.

Apart from isolated moments, it was a game of turnovers, missed opportunities and a terrible absence of anything resembling class. Compliment the grunt, but…

It was chaos. Every breakdown was a lottery, an ugly dogfight. The longer it went on, the more Australia became serial offenders. That game-clinching penalty from Russell was on the back of multiple Wallaby breakdown offences.

There were some seriously creative and pacy players out there but we hardly saw them. Precious little fast ball, precious little buzz from two teams who are well capable of excitement. Neither attack sparked never mind fired. The final whistle came as something of a blessing.

Nations Championship: Scotland hang on for scrappy win over Australia - reaction

Million big hits but awful absence of quality

Scotland suffered a blow even before the first whistle when captain Sione Tuipulotu was ruled out with a knee injury. Tom Jordan replaced him in the midfield and Rory Darge took over the leadership role.

Both are stand-up operators, but any Scotland team without Tuipulotu is a weaker outfit.

Huge question marks hung over the pair before the start - Scotland having been blown away by the All Blacks last weekend as the Wallabies went down in flames at Twickenham.

Depending on how it went - Scotland were warm favourites - this was going to be some sort of redemption for one and all sorts of retribution for the other. All of that was in the balance right until the end.

Scotland now move above Wales into fourth in the northern hemisphere table, but their lack of a bonus point on Sunday could cost them. They'll take the win, though.

In the scrappiest encounter, the home side drew first blood. They owned the ball in the early moments, wasted one opportunity to score off a lineout maul, but then struck at the second time of asking.

Finn Russell started it all with a lovely grubber that had Carter Gordon in trouble. It eventually led to a scrum and men over for Scotland. An isolated Fagerson on the right touchline had been calling for it for what must have felt like an age to him. When it did come, he had the easiest job of sliding over.

Russell missed the conversion, but he missed something - or somebody - else just after and it proved costly. One of the many things holding Scotland back is how easy they are to score against - and here was another case for the prosecution.

Rob Valetini and Gordon helped put the Wallabies on the front foot but, when they swept to the left touchline, the whole thing might have come to a halt had Russell made his tackle on Potter. He didn't - and the wing ran on to finish with class.

Scotland thought they'd scored just after but the ball was deemed out of play - a marginal call - when Kyle Steyn mid-air volleyed to Graham, who touched down.

Another injury befell the Scots midway through the opening half when Scott Cummings was replaced by Max Williamson.

The Scots scored their second try soon after. Too much power in the phases and Dempsey drove over against the nation he once represented.

Russell made it 12-5 and it stayed that way despite Billy Pollard being driven over from a lineout maul. The Wallabies were done for obstruction.

The pre-match billing talked about a thrilling try-fest but it was low-key and error-strewn. You expected Scotland to bring their usual ambition but, if anything, they were conservative.

The Wallabies tried to play more rugby, but their game was riddled with mistakes, too. It was chaos out there for large parts of it. Bodies everywhere. A million big hits. Just an awful absence of quality.

Paris on Friday, this was not. Cardiff on Sunday, it was not either.

Pollard got binned for going high on Blair Kinghorn early in the new half but Scotland could do nothing in those precious 10 minutes. They butchered a big opportunity from a close-range lineout - losing their own throw - then won it back and got turned over at the breakdown.

Scotland played much of the second half in Aussie territory but only had those three Russell points to show for it. Just as well.

Australia scored in the last seconds when Jorgensen ran in after a beautiful offload from Jeremy Williams. Ben Donaldson put over the conversion to make it 15-12. Too little, too late for the visitors. Just. Scotland survived.

After two days of Nations Championship rugby that will live long in the memory, this one will have faded in the time it took fans to reach the car park.

'When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style'

articles.title: Nations Championship: Scotland edge out Australia at Murrayfield to move above Wales in  Northern Hemisphere table
articles.summary: Scotland beat Australia 15-12 but couldn't secure a bonus point; Head coach Gregor Townsend said: "Defensively, that's one of the best performances I've seen in the last couple of years"; Scotland move above Wales into fourth in the Northern Hemisphere table
articles.body:
First-half scores from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave the Scots the edge at the break, with Harry Potter responding for the Wallabies.

Finn Russell's late penalty eventually gave the Scots some breathing space before Max Jorgensen's 80th-minute try offered the visitors a glimmer of hope but the Scots held on for a win that elevated them above Wales into fourth place in the Northern Hemisphere table.

"When we saw the rain half an hour before kick off, you still hope you'll be able to move the ball. You could tell defences were coming off the line a bit quicker, knowing they could pressure the ball carrier," Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend told ITV

"Both teams had to adjust and I thought we did that well. Defensively, that's one of the best performances I've seen in the last couple of years. Set after set we were putting them under pressure.

"We were on that edge of physicality but disciplined, hitting hard in the tackle, putting pressure on, listening to the referee, getting back onside. That makes it hard for the opposition to get into our 22m, which was a learning from last week.

"It was just constant effort. Today, we showed we can play another game, too."

articles.title: Gregor Townsend hails Scotland's defence in Australia 'arm wrestle'
articles.summary: Scotland's Nations Championship win over Australia was far from a classic, but head coach Gregor Townsend says it was one of his side's best defensive performances in recent years.
articles.body:
Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend hailed his team's defensive efforts after they edged past Australia in a Nations Championship "arm wrestle" at Murrayfield.

Off the back of being dismantled by New Zealand last weekend, in which they failed to score a second half point, the spotlight fell on Scotland's leaky defence.

But on a chilly and damp Edinburgh day where physicality was king, they delivered a much-needed win and showed they are capable of winning ugly.

Even so, Townsend's side didn't make it easy.

Max Jorgensen's late converted try gave the Wallabies hope, and with the clock in the red, the visitors broke from their own half.

Murrayfield held its breath, but Darcy Graham hauled Australia full-back Tom Wright into touch with a superb tackle.

"When we saw the rain half an hour before kick-off, you still hope you'll be able to move the ball," Townsend said.

"You could tell defences were coming off the line a bit quicker, knowing they could pressure the ball carrier.

"Both teams had to adjust and I thought we did that well. Defensively, that's one of the best performances I've seen in the last couple of years. Set after set we were putting them under pressure.

"We were on that edge of physicality but disciplined, hitting hard in the tackle, putting pressure on, listening to the referee, getting back onside. That makes it hard for the opposition to get into our 22m, which was a learning from last week.

"It was just constant effort. Today, we showed we can play another game, too."

Final whistle a blessing as Scotland edge dull Test against Australia

Nations Championship: Scotland hang on for scrappy win over Australia - as it happened

Leading 12-5 at half-time, there was one eye on whether Scotland could clinch a bonus-point victory that would have both boosted their points difference and helped their chances of climbing the northern hemisphere table with Japan to come on Saturday.

However, it soon became apparent that would not be forthcoming in a match that will not live long in the memory.

"It was about winning at all costs today," former Scotland prop Peter Wright said.

"We hoped we might get something quite end-to-end, 50 points to 48, loads of tries, but to come out on the right end of a war of attrition like that, it's a good feeling.

"When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style at any sport. We just want to get victories under our belt.

"It was a bad game last week so getting some momentum going into the Japan game next week was really important.

In the absence of Sione Tuipulotu, who was ruled out of playing against the country of his birth with a knee injury, Rory Darge captained Scotland and led from the front with a player-of-the-match display.

The Glasgow Warriors flanker was immense in contact and at the breakdown, and also had the presence of mind to tell Finn Russell to kick at goal instead of going to the corner in the closing stages.

The resulting three points put Scotland 10 points in front and proved to be the winning score.

Townsend praised the performance his stand-in skipper, while also pointing to a wider effort defensively.

"You know the opposition will get phases of attack and we'll have to defend. Rory with his tackling, with his effort and his post-tackle presence really helps us.

"There were a lot of other players that stood up physically. The shots that were going in, the effort going in was outstanding."

And Darge himself was heartened by how Scotland responded to the All Blacks loss.

"We were disappointed after last week's performance," he said.

"A lot of that disappointment was with the physical side of the game and we did that really well.

"It was a bit of an arm wrestle, the conditions played their part. We know they want to throw the ball around, we like to play an attacking style but today was a battle of the defences."

'When you're Scottish, winning's always good. We very rarely win in style'

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Wales need to back up All Blacks win in Nations Championship
articles.summary: Wales head coach Steve Tandy challenges his side to build on their historic win against New Zealand when they host Australia next Saturday.
articles.body:
Wales head coach Steve Tandy has challenged his side to back up their wonderful win against New Zealand when they host Australia next weekend.

After beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years with the 35-28 win at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales face the final game of the Nations Championship - before the play-offs - against the Wallabies on Saturday evening (20:10 BST).

Tandy says Wales will attempt not to dwell on what they achieved on Saturday against New Zealand as they aim for a third successive home win.

"We have to keep going and we've got a massive game against Australia next weekend," said Tandy.

"It's going to be a different kind of test for us after we have had back-to-back home wins.

"We've gone up another notch or another couple of levels, so it's important we back that up. It's about making sure when we come in that we're ready to work."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and Sports Extra on BBC Sounds

After defeat to England, Australia lost 15-12 against Scotland on Sunday, a result which leaves Wales fifth in the northern hemisphere table.

Wales are behind behind Gregor Townsend's side on points difference with Scotland finishing their campaign against Japan.

Tandy's side have won three out of five games in the Nations Championship against Fiji, Japan and New Zealand with defeats in the summer against Argentina and South Africa.

Captain Dewi Lake has highlighted what has changed for this campaign to enable Wales to defeat New Zealand and rise one place in the world rankings to ninth.

"Our skills are better and I think we're a better team which is credit to Steve and his coaches," said Lake.

"I think the belief is also different and the mindset has shifted.

"We've spoken about it a lot and it's probably easy sometimes to say we've changed our mindset and believe in ourselves.

"It feels different. Everybody has come in with a voice and a belief and are challenging each other to get better. Ultimately that's what grows a group quickly."

Reality dawns after Wales dared to dream

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

Young players need space to grow - Tandy

Tandy believes Wales' young players need to be given the environment to express themselves.

"There's a young group that needed care," Tandy said.

"Those connection pieces we speak about a lot and it's something we pride ourselves on."

He highlighted players like Eddie James, Dan Edwards and Sam Costelow, among those gaining caps and growing in confidence.

"It's trying to give them the freedom to play, because it's a tough place to play in Wales when things are not going right," the Wales head coach added.

"They're young men and we want these players to go out there and play with freedom.

"They need to have that and we believe in that support for them, because sometimes it may be a little bit of a burden.

"We've got to make sure these boys have a safe space."

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Sam Prendergast cited for tackle as Dan Sheehan returns
articles.summary: Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast is in danger of missing Saturday's Nations Championship match against South Africa after being cited for a tackle against Fiji.
articles.body:
Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast is in danger of missing Saturday's Nations Championship match against South Africa after being cited for a tackle against Fiji.

Prendergast will face a disciplinary process for a hip-drop tackle on Fijian captain Peceli Yato in the first half of Ireland's 43-15 win in Dublin on Saturday.

The technique, when a tackling player drops their hips and bodyweight on to the ball-carrier's legs, was outlawed by World Rugby before November's internationals and the 23-year-old is the first player to be cited over its use in a game.

If found guilty and he accepts the verdict, Prendergast could face a pre-determined sanction through the Six Nations' expedited disciplinary process.

However, if he does not accept the charge then he would be referred to a panel to determine any possible outcome.

Australia's Angus Bell was yellow carded for a hip-drop tackle against England, but Prendergast's alleged offence was not penalised by match officials during the match.

If Prendergast receives a suspension, Connacht fly-half Ciaran Frawley would be the prime candidate to start against the Springboks on Saturday [16:40 GMT].

Ulster's Jamie Benson, who has yet to be capped at international level, is also an option for Farrell.

'We know we can do it' - Farrell eyes Springbok scalp

South Africa recall Etzebeth for Ireland match

Fiji 'did Ireland a favour' before South Africa game

Sheehan set for return against Springboks

In better news for Ireland, captain Dan Sheehan is set to return for the game against the back-to-back world champions at the Aviva Stadium after he completed return to play protocols.

Sheehan - who is deputising for regular skipper Caelan Doris - missed Saturday's win over Fiji after sustaining a concussion in the defeat of Argentina on 6 November.

But in a squad update issued on Monday, the Irish Rugby Football Union (IRFU) said Sheehan will return to full training this week before the Springboks' visit to Dublin.

Ulster back row James McNabney is unavailable while he undergoes 12-day return to play protocols after sustaining a head injury that prematurely ended his eye-catching debut off the bench against the Fijians.

Tight-head prop Sam Illo is a doubt as he enters the return to play process, while utility back Jamie Osborne is ruled out with a pectoral injury that forced him off in the opening minutes of the Fiji game.

If Illo misses the Springboks game, Farrell has Thomas Clarkson and Tom O'Toole as back-up tight-head options with Tadhg Furlong expected to start.

Farrell will name his team to face the back-to-back world champions at 14:00 GMT on Thursday.

South Africa won last year's meeting 24-13 in Dublin but lost to France in Paris last weekend.

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: Springboks recall record cap holder Eben Etzebeth for Nations Championship game
articles.summary: South Africa record cap holder Eben Etzebeth is recalled for Saturday's much-anticipated Nations Championship game against Ireland in Dublin.
articles.body:
South Africa record cap holder Eben Etzebeth has been recalled for Saturday's much-anticipated Nations Championship game against Ireland in Dublin.

Etzebeth, 35, missed the Springboks' win over Italy and defeat by France because of injury, but replaces Lood de Jager to earn a record-extending 148th Test cap alongside Ruan Nortje in the world champions' second row.

Cameron Hanekom is named at number eight, replacing Jasper Wiese, who is facing a possible ban after being sent off for a dangerous clear-out in the France game .

Hanekom joins captain Siya Kolisi and two-time World Rugby player of the year Pieter-Steph du Toit in the back row, with Marco van Staden replacing Hanekom on the bench.

Ox Nche, Malcolm Marx and Wilco Louw are named as the starting front row at the Aviva Stadium (16:40 GMT).

Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus also named Nche, Marx and Louw to start the France game but swapped them out for Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Gerhard Steenekamp and Thomas du Toit shortly before kick-off at the Stade de France.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Erasmus defended that decision.

"We saw the team France had selected and looked at the players we were going to face," he said.

"We probably could have made the changes when they announced their side on Thursday, but the regulations allow you to change the team the following morning before the game.

"We thought, 'Let's get Jan-Hendrik Wessels, Thomas du Toit and Gerhard Steenekamp out there'. Maybe we'll need them next year at the World Cup, under pressure, starting a big Test match for us against one of the best scrummaging packs.

"That was the thinking behind it. We wanted to expose those guys to that pressure and give them that experience."

Erasmus added: "If people are going to keep getting upset about it, then I apologise. But I'm not apologising for doing it. I'm apologising because you're probably going to keep getting upset about it!

"If Ireland name a side on Thursday and that we didn't think they were going to play, we might make some changes."

Prendergast cited and could miss South Africa game

'We know we can do it' - Farrell eyes Springbok scalp

Fiji 'did Ireland a favour' before South Africa game

Fly-half Manie Libbok, whose missed conversion attempt cost the Boks a draw against France, is dropped, with Canan Moodie called into the matchday squad, while Grant Williams replaces Cobus Reinach as the back-up scrum-half.

Erasmus has stuck with the backline that started in Paris. Damian Willemse, Kurt-Lee Arendse and Ethan Hooker are retained in the back three with Jesse Kriel and Damian de Allende again lining out in midfield.

Star fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu and Morne van den Berg continue their half-back partnership.

Reflecting on last week's loss, Erasmus said: "We let ourselves and the country down, and we are determined to fix the mistakes that cost us, so we'll leave no stone unturned to ensure that we play according to our standards this weekend.

"The coaches and the entire squad took a good look at ourselves over the last few days and we know what we did wrong and what we have to improve on, so we know what we have to do this week, and we'll give everything at training and on the field on the weekend."

South Africa sit second in the Nations Championship southern hemisphere standings, a point adrift of New Zealand.

A South Africa win over Ireland coupled with England beating the All Blacks (Saturday, 14:10 GMT) would be enough for Erasmus' side to seal a place in the 29 November final against the top-ranked northern hemisphere side at Twickenham.

The Springboks won 24-13 in Dublin last year, their first victory over Ireland since 2012.

South Africa: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, De Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Van den Berg; Nche, Marx, Louw, Etzebeth, Nortje, Kolisi (capt), PS Du Toit, Hanekom.

Replacements: Wessels, Steenekamp, T du Toit, De Jager, De Villiers, Van Staden, Williams, Moodie.

articles.title: England v New Zealand: All Blacks coach Dave Rennie says team 'let the country down' in Wales defeat
articles.summary: New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie demands a reaction against England, as he acknowledges the All Blacks "let the country down" by losing to Wales.
articles.body:
New Zealand head coach Dave Rennie has demanded a reaction against England on Saturday after saying the All Blacks "let the country down" in their historic defeat by Wales.

In one of the great upsets of the professional era, New Zealand lost 35-28 in Cardiff at the weekend, a first defeat against the Welsh in 73 years.

New Zealand will face an in-form England in Twickenham as they look to avoid back-to-back Nations Championship losses, with Rennie vowing not to brush the Wales result "under the carpet".

"It's important we poke each other in the chest at the start of the week," Rennie said.

"You have to front up and take things on the chin, all of us. Come Saturday, our mindset will be fully on England and our job is to perform.

"We will be highly motivated for the weekend, but we won't brush the [Wales] result under the carpet.

"[The players] are feeling it. They know we let ourselves down and we let the country down."

The Botham hiding in plain sight - Wales' unlikely All Blacks hero

England are favourites against All Blacks, and fearless Wales are an inspiration

Time for WRU to match team's leadership - Davies

Rennie paid tribute to a "clinical and passionate" Wales team, but he lamented his side's uncharacteristic wastefulness when camped in Welsh territory in the final quarter of the game.

"We are all reflecting on what we could do better. You can't just blame it on the guys who take the field," Rennie said.

"It's disappointing and not good enough, but we've got to learn from it and bottle up the feeling post-game, because it hurts, and we have some pretty big footy coming up in the next few weeks and next year.

"I should have done a better job last week. We picked a side that was a very good side and a side I was really confident that if we played to our potential would perform well.

"But I also knew [Wales] had a really strong coaching group, smart, and were a passionate nation playing at home."

Rennie is set to call upon a host of big-name players for the match at Allianz Stadium as the All Blacks look to avenge their defeat in Twickenham this time last year.

Damian McKenzie, Jordie Barrett, Codie Taylor and Cam Roigard will all return, while star wing Will Jordan is in the selection mix after a hamstring problem.

However, Quinn Tupaea, a fixture in the team throughout 2026 at outside centre, needs surgery on a thumb injury and will be out for the next 10 weeks.

"Playing England at Twickenham is always a big occasion, and we are playing a side who is in good form," added Rennie.

"They can hurt you up front, they bring a lot of line speed defensively, and they've been really sharp attack-wise. They are playing a lot of footy and we are well aware of that.

"The loss on the weekend creates a little bit more edge, but I wouldn't say we are going to be more motivated than we would have been. England at Twickenham is always a tough assignment."

articles.title: James Botham: Wales' unlikely hero in historic win over New Zealand
articles.summary: James Botham is accustomed to working away from the spotlight, but his performance could not be denied against New Zealand.
articles.body:
James Botham lay sprawled on the Principality Stadium turf, pain and exhaustion etched across his face.

Whenever the whistle blew, the Wales flanker in the red scrum cap took an age to rise. Precious seconds to recover. Nobody counts tackles when the ball is dead.

But when play resumed, he was everywhere. Tackling, scrambling, hitting the deck and springing back up.

By the final whistle, Botham had helped Wales beat New Zealand for the first time in 73 years. He was man of the match. And as the celebrations began, the tears flowed.

Quite an afternoon for a player accustomed to working away from the spotlight.

Keeping a Botham out of the headlines was always going to be difficult.

His grandfather, Lord Ian Botham , is one of Britain's great sporting celebrities. Outspoken, charismatic and capable of turning cricket matches almost single-handedly, he is box-office.

His game is built on tackles, chasing, wrestling and relentless graft. Few positions in rugby are less glamorous than blind-side flanker.

But on Saturday, Wales' number six was the star of the show.

Botham's introduction to international rugby could hardly have been less glamorous.

He made his Wales debut against Georgia at an empty Parc y Scarlets in November 2020, with Covid-19 restrictions keeping supporters away.

His grandfather always believed he would play for Wales, but getting there was one thing. Staying there proved harder.

Part of Wales' Six Nations-winning squad in 2021, Botham subsequently spent more than two and a half years away from the international side.

Injuries and competition played their part. But perhaps his greatest qualities were not always easy to appreciate.

His game was built less on spectacular breaks than on repeated collisions, defensive work and battles at the breakdown.

In that respect, his career echoes another Cardiff flanker, Josh Navidi.

Navidi made his Wales debut in 2013 but waited four years for his second cap.

Long regarded as an outstanding regional player rather than an international star, his strength, work rate and dominance in contact eventually made him indispensable to Wales.

He won 33 caps and toured with the British and Irish Lions.

Botham has followed a similar path. A gifted athlete, his greatest strengths are not always obvious from the stands or on television.

"I remember seeing him when he first came to Cardiff," said the former Wales and Lions captain.

"His footwork for contact was amazing, just how explosive he was over five, ten metres."

Warburton believes Botham has the attributes of a top international blindside flanker.

"Really strong in contact. Gets great numbers in the gym. He's fast. He's fit. He's probably the best athlete that Wales have in the back row," Warburton added.

One training session with Botham helped convince Warburton his own playing days were numbered.

"I was linked up with James Botham and that's when I realised the flame had gone," he recalled.

"He was full beans going for it and I remember thinking, in the nicest way, I don't care."

For a player whose career was built on an insatiable appetite for physical confrontation, it was telling.

Warburton realised the aggression and hunger that had driven him to the top were gone.

Botham, meanwhile, was just getting started.

Former Wales hooker Scott Baldwin shared a room with Botham on a Barbarians tour, where the social traditions are almost as famous as the rugby.

After a few drinks one evening, Botham decided he still needed a fitness session, so he ran a mile to a nearby pitch, completed his drills and jogged back to rejoin his team-mates.

"He was fully committed to the social, but he had to get his bit in," Baldwin recalled.

Baldwin believes that dedication is evident on the field, even if it often goes unnoticed.

"We'd probably underestimate how much work he gets through every game," he added. "His ability to slow ball down is next level."

And then there is his willingness to chase lost causes: "He's the kid that will chase every kick, whether he's going to get there or not."

Against New Zealand, that unseen work was impossible to ignore.

Botham made 30 tackles as Wales ended 73 years of hurt against the All Blacks. Only Dafydd Jenkins (38) and Jac Morgan (31) made more.

But his most remarkable contribution was a tackle that barely registered in the statistics.

With New Zealand threatening the Welsh line, Botham somehow got his knee beneath hooker Asafo Aumua, preventing what looked like a certain try.

An extraordinary intervention from a player who appeared to be running on empty.

Wales scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams, who kicked the ball into touch to seal the victory, was impressed.

"You could tell from the weekend he was a Test match animal," he said.

"He's a mental athlete as well. He's fit, he's fast, and he was everywhere, really, wasn't he?"

Time for WRU to match team's leadership - Sir Gerald

Reality dawns after Wales dared to dream

Wales must look to back up All Blacks win - Tandy

Warburton believes Botham has made his case to become Wales' established blindside flanker.

"I think he's definitely stamped down his name at six," he said.

At 28, Botham has taken the long road to becoming an overnight success. With his first child due this week, it promises to be a momentous few days off the field, too.

His surname will always invite comparisons. Any profile of James will inevitably mention his grandfather. This one, after all, has done exactly that.

But there was nothing inherited about the tackles, the exhaustion or the tears at the final whistle.

On Saturday, James Botham was the star of his own story.

articles.title: Nations Championship: England's Will Joseph in line to start against New Zealand
articles.summary: England's Will Joseph is in line to retain his place for Saturday's blockbuster Nations Championship meeting with New Zealand after scoring five tries against Japan.
articles.body:
England's Will Joseph is in line to retain his place for Saturday's blockbuster Nations Championship meeting with New Zealand after scoring five tries against Japan.

In the absence of the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Joseph is understood to be in pole position to reprise his role on the wing after a performance packed with pace and finishing ability.

Joseph scored a hat-trick inside the first 19 minutes, on the way to becoming only the fifth England men's player to score five tries in one match.

He also headed the team's charts for metres carried (224) and top speed (21.7mph).

The 24-year-old won his second Test cap in Saturday's 78-15 thrashing of the Brave Blossoms, four and half years after making his debut as a teenager.

After a late cameo as a replacement in England's second Test win over Australia in July 2022, Joseph struggled to fulfil his promise. Boyhood club London Irish went into liquidation and a stint at Harlequins was hampered by injury and a lack of game time.

However, Joseph has been a key part of Gloucester's resurgence this season and, watched by elder brother and former England centre Jonathan Joseph, he made a sensational return to international rugby at Allianz Stadium last weekend.

England are favourites against All Blacks - Matt Dawson column

Nations Championship final round - who needs what?

"He is just so fast. He doesn't look too fast in the first two steps and then he is just gone. He gets away from people," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live of Joseph's ability.

"He floats, doesn't he?" added England team-mate Ben Earl to BBC Sport.

"The way he carries himself, he does really move like his brother. They are so, so similar."

With Feyi-Waboso ruled out of the autumn by an ankle injury, Cadan Murley is the other specialist wing in England's squad vying with Joseph for a spot alongside likely first-choice Tommy Freeman in the back three.

After victories over Australia and Japan this autumn, England are second in the Nations Championship northern hemisphere standings and in line for a play-off meeting with South Africa on finals weekend on 27-29 November.

However, that could change considerably, with New Zealand leading the southern hemisphere table and second-place South Africa taking on Ireland, who are behind England only on points difference.

articles.title: Rassie Erasmus: World Rugby to review South Africa head coach's extraordinary comments about double standards from officials
articles.summary: Rassie Erasmus claimed officials missed as many as 17 illegal tackles against his side in their defeat by France, and asked if "manipulation" of the result could be behind the reason not to look at the incidents; Springboks boss also thinks Ireland's Sam Prendergast will play on Saturday
articles.body:
Not for the first time, Erasmus delivered a strikingly outspoken press conference on Monday, suggesting officials missed 17 illegal tackles against his side in their narrow loss to France , going as far as to question whether "manipulation" of the result is behind why incidents such as these are not picked up by officials during matches.

He also predicted that a "technicality" will emerge that sees Ireland's Sam Prendergast free to play Saturday's game against South Africa, after the fly-half was cited for a hip-drop tackle in his side's win over Fiji last weekend.

Erasmus has found himself in hot water for publicly admonishing the performances of officials in the past. In 2021, he was banned from all rugby activity for two months for his behaviour towards match officials during his side's Test series against the British and Irish Lions, during which he released an hour-long video critiquing the referee's display in the first Test.

On Monday, Erasmus questioned why many of France's knee-drop tackles he believed to be illegal were not reviewed by the video referee.

"Let's say 11 of those were at least a penalty and three I thought was at least three yellow cards. And not one was sanctioned and not one was showed out or cited," Erasmus said in widely-reported quotes.

"I'll send you the playlist but I'll get into trouble… So I can't send the playlist to anybody and we can only send five clips to World Rugby. So we'll probably query it but the answer will probably be: 'Yes, it was a mistake, it should have been penalised'.

"On numerous times we mentioned to the referee 'we think there's a knee-drop tackle'. I'm saying to you my feeling is that knee-drop tackles is out. They happened 17 times in our game. Not one was penalised."

"And if the TMO didn't see it, then maybe technology must be better. If he saw it and ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result? Or players getting injured?

"So, all I'm asking is don't take the TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

In response to Sky Sports News , World Rugby will review Erasmus' comments in the context of the match official abuse sanction framework that was introduced earlier this year.

That process was brought in to reduce comments that lead to "the unacceptable increase in abuse and threats towards match officials."

Under this framework, an independent three-person panel will review the comments to determine if they were made with a view to undermining confidence in officials, with potential punishments including multiple match bans.

Erasmus predicts Prendergast will play despite 'terrible' tackle

It is not yet known if Ireland fly-half Prendergast will be available for Saturday's crunch Nations Championship meeting at Dublin's Aviva Stadium, after he was cited for an alleged illegal hip-drop tackle against Fiji .

Despite the lack of ruling, Erasmus made it clear that he does not expect Prendergast to be penalised.

"We are in the northern hemisphere," Erasmus said. "I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play.

"We all thought it's an immediate red card. Everybody watched the game live because that's exactly what they said the hip-drop tackle is," he said.

"I swear I'm not moaning. I'm just trying to give you a perspective of somebody who comes and plays, for example, in France or in Ireland."

Ireland and South Africa have enjoyed an intense and at times fraught rivalry in recent years, with Ireland head coach Andy Farrell winning three of his five meetings against the Springboks.

However, South Africa were victorious in the most recent chapter of the rivalry, winning in Dublin a year ago in a game which saw five Irish players carded.

Should he be available, Prendergast would be expected to start at No 10 on Saturday, something Erasmus believes would not be fair given his tackle last weekend.

"It's difficult to understand when the TMO sits there and he sees that," he said.

"And it was something we discussed at the World Rugby meeting, and the examples of how it is was shown over and over, and we all had input.

"Somebody sees that and he decides there's nothing wrong with that."

articles.title: Ireland v South Africa: 'Is that not match fixing?' - Rassie Erasmus questions officiating
articles.summary: South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus predicts Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast will not face a ban after being cited, and questions standards in officiating.
articles.body:
South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has predicted Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast will not face a ban after being cited, and questioned what he perceived as double standards in officiating to the point where he asked: "is that not match-fixing?"

Prendergast became the first player to be cited under World Rugby's new regulations for a hip-drop tackle against Fiji and could be banned for Saturday's Nations Championship match.

Speaking at a media conference on Monday, Erasmus said the 23-year-old's tackle was "terrible", but he believes Prendergast will be free to play against the Springboks in Dublin because of a "technicality".

The 54-year-old also added that he thought it was an "immediate red card" when he saw the tackle occur in the first half of Ireland's 43-15 win, but it was not penalised in-game by referee Angus Gardner or by the television match official Mike Adamson.

"I must say the right words now. We are in the northern hemisphere. I think there is going to be a technicality and he is going to play," Erasmus said when asked about Prendergast being cited.

When he was asked to elaborate on what he meant by a "technicality", Erasmus said that, while he is "not a legal guy", "it never seems to go our way".

"I'm not saying anybody's doing anything wrong. I'm just not expecting him to get [suspended] - I think he'll play on Saturday," Erasmus said.

World Rugby has been approached for comment by BBC Sport over Erasmus' comments.

Prendergast cited and could miss South Africa game

SA recall Etzebeth as Erasmus defends late changes

Erasmus, who said "I swear I'm not moaning", also pointed to how Ireland prop Tadhg Furlong avoided punishment for an alleged groin grab in Leinster's United Rugby Championship win over Munster in October.

Last year, South Africa prop Jan-Hendrik Wessels was handed a nine-match ban for a similar offence and missed November's matches for the Springboks.

"Tadhg got off free for the same thing Jan-Hendrik did. I don't want to go into details because I'm not a legal person, but from a South African point of view, that hurt," added Erasmus.

"I'm telling you now for any neutral - and I'm not saying the neutrals are right - but for anybody that looks at that situation on exactly the same two things that happened, one guy's word was taken, and another guy's word was not taken.

"One guy got nine weeks. He didn't play for the Springboks, and the other guy played the next weekend. That's all I'm saying."

In 2021, when he was South Africa's director of rugby, Erasmus was banned for two months by World Rugby for an hour-long video criticising the refereeing in the Springboks' first-Test defeat by the British and Irish Lions.

World Rugby found the video contained "multiple abusive and insulting comments and attacks on the officials".

The following year, he received a two-match ban for a series of tweets criticising officials in a defeat by France.

Erasmus said there had been a meeting with World Rugby over the implementation of new laws surrounding the hip-drop and knee-drop tackle for November's internationals, which Ireland and France coaches didn't attend.

Hip and knee-drop tackles are when the tackling player drops their body weight on the legs of the ball carrier, and Fiji captain Peceli Yato was eventually forced off with an injury against Ireland after he initially continued following Prendergast's tackle.

South Africa head into this weekend's game in Dublin off the back of a narrow 21-19 defeat by France at the Stade de France on Saturday.

After saying he would get in trouble if he showed video evidence, Erasmus said that 17 hip-drop or knee-drop tackles by French players were not penalised by match referee Andrea Piardi or the TMO Matteo Liperini in Paris - 11 of which he thought were penalties and three which he felt should have been yellow cards.

Erasmus said his comments were "not an accusation" about the officials, and questioned World Rugby's prerogative to limit interruptions from the TMO.

"I'm saying if he didn't see it, it must be a technology problem. If he saw it and decided not to act on it, is that not match-fixing?" Erasmus added.

"Is that not interfering with the outcome of a game if you see this injury that happened there, a knee-drop tackle happened there, and it's been decided that knee-drop tackles are out?"

Erasmus said his players spoke to Piardi and the officials about the number of knee-drop tackles, and he doubled down on his views over the lack of intervention from the TMO.

"They happened 17 in our games. Not one was penalised even," Erasmus said.

"If the TMO didn't see it, maybe then technology must be better. If he saw it and he ignored it, what does that boil down to? Manipulation of the game or the result or injured players getting injured.

"So all I'm asking, don't take TMOs out and discourage them to get involved. Then the wrong team will win and players will get injured. That's all I'm saying."

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Five key areas for Steve Tandy's side to back up All Blacks win
articles.summary: After stunning New Zealand on a historic afternoon in Cardiff, Wales must return to earth against Australia in the Nations Championship.
articles.body:
As the dust settles on Wales' historic victory over New Zealand, work is under way to secure another major scalp.

Steve Tandy's side ensured their place in history by ending the 73-year wait for a win against the All Blacks.

Now they must back up what many are describing as the one of the greatest results in Welsh rugby history by beating Australia in Cardiff on Saturday.

Wales have won just one of their past five meetings with the Wallabies and are without a victory over them in Cardiff since 2021.

But victory would complete only their second ever clean sweep of autumn internationals following the statement win on Saturday.

"[Beating the All Blacks] wasn't even by fluke, that's the nicest thing," former Wales centre Tom Shanklin told the Scrum V podcast.

"It wasn't like there were two or three cards for New Zealand. Wales did it the hard way and deserved to win."

So what must Wales get right this week on the final weekend of the Nations Championship group stage?

Time for WRU to match team's leadership - Davies

Inside Wales' dressing room - how Lake inspired history

Not often can rugby results be genuinely described as historic, but the euphoria surrounding a first win over New Zealand since 1953 can easily be excused.

Players and fans broke down in tears at the final whistle on Saturday, as much in surprise as relief. The wait to beat the All Blacks again has been agonising.

But Tandy now has the immensely tough challenge of lifting his players once again to somewhere near that emotional and physical peak.

"Wales need to have that same mindset and belief, that's the biggest task after that emotional high," said Shanklin.

"I think they will be alright. Games like this can change your career [and] Australia are there for the taking."

Former Wales fly-half James Hook added: "We were in a world of pain after going out of the [2007] World Cup, then we go to Twickenham and win when nobody believed we could. The week after against Scotland, we just didn't think we could lose - and we didn't.

"These boys will go into that game against Australia and will feel that they can't lose and hopefully, the crowd gives them the ovation they deserve."

Victory over New Zealand was inspired by Wales' epic defensive stand.

Beauden Barrett said it felt like New Zealand were running into a red brick wall as Wales racked up a remarkable 346 tackles.

Tandy brought in ex-Glasgow defence coach Peter Murchie during the summer to work alongside contact specialist Dan Lydiate and the move is paying off.

Shanklin believes the mind-set and physical comitment was reminiscent of the demands of Grand Slam-winning defence coach Shaun Edwards.

"There was the drive and mindset to keep them out and make big hits," he said.

"There was one player on the floor and the rest in the defensive line.

"They got back up every single time, nobody was slow. Every time the All Blacks looked up there was a red wall."

Australia may have lost their past four Tests and have just one victory in six - albeit against world champions South Africa - but they have regularly been free-scoring against Wales, including eight tries on their most recent trip to Cardiff in 2024.

The Botham hiding in plain sight - Wales' unlikely hero

Wales must look to back up All Blacks win - Tandy

Wales' attack finally sparked as they racked up a record try tally against New Zealand in Cardiff.

Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit crossed as Wales scored five tries against the All Blacks for the first time.

After labouring against Japan, Anscombe said New Zealand looked "shell-shocked" by the accuracy and physicality of the Welsh attack.

Shanklin added: "Wales nailed it. We saw them play with attacking options, width, tempo and quick ball.

"The attack looked slick with options everywhere. Nobody was running on their own and there was a tip-on either inside or outside. Wales made the right decisions and were clever in how they attacked."

At the heart of that impressive attacking was fly-half Sam Costelow.

His place in the Wales team was in serious doubt following the uninspiring result against Japan a week earlier.

But Tandy ignored calls for Dan Edwards to take back the number ten 10 jersey and kept faith in the Scarlets fly-half.

Costelow responded with his best international performance, sparking Wales and crucially kicking all five conversions.

"I am rapt for Costy because he has been through the wars with Wales," said fellow Scarlet and former Wales fly-half Gareth Anscombe.

"He has taken a battering at times. He has been in the team for a while and came in at a young age when things were starting to turn the other way.

"It's tough as a 10 when you are sitting behind a team that is getting dominated up front. It's tough to pull rabbits out of the hat."

Shane Williams was among those calling for consistency in selection.

But Edwards, who started last season's wins against Italy and Fiji, made a telling contribution off the bench, not least when he denied Leicester Fainga'anuku a try.

Anscombe added: "Dan brings energy so potentially suits coming off the bench, particularly if Wales are trying to chase the game with his ability to use his legs to cause trouble."

As well as fly-half, Tandy faces a selection dilemma in his back-row having rung changes between the Tests against Japan and New Zealand.

Taine Basham hugely impressed against the All Blacks, as did Taine Plumtree off the bench, but Aaron Wainwright could be available following an ankle injury.

And while Alex Mann has been a regular first-choice at number six, his Cardiff team-mate James Botham took his place with a man of the match display on Saturday.

"Sometimes you have guys that play well at regional level [but] when they play at the Test arena they go up a couple of notches. Botham is like that," said Anscombe.

"He was physical, made tackles and got through so much work. He has to be a regular in the back-row, even though they are blessed with options."

articles.title: Will Joseph: England winger set to start against New Zealand after remarkable four-year journey to national side comeback
articles.summary: Sky Sports looks at Will Joseph's sensational return to the England fold four years after making his first cap; Joseph has overcome injuries, the liquidation of his boyhood club and a loss of hearing in one ear all while caring for his twin; he is set to start vs New Zealand
articles.body:
The winger is only the fifth player in England history to score five times in a Test match - managing the feat in his first appearance since 2022 - with the display set to have secured him a starting berth in the crucial Nations Championship clash against New Zealand on Saturday.

His return marked the culmination of a odyssey back into Steve Borthwick's side that has seen him battle injury, permanent hearing loss in one ear and the liquidation of his boyhood club - all while caring for his twin brother, Alex, who suffers with serious health issues and severe learning difficulties.

"I've been on a bit of a journey from when I was first here," Joseph told Sky Sports. " I've learned a lot about myself, and I've got a better understanding of what it takes to probably be in this environment, and to be at this level."

Joseph's "journey" has seen him overcome more in four years than many players face over the course of their entire lives - let alone their careers.

Joseph: Loss of hearing jeopardised my career

After a promising beginning to his professional career with boyhood club London Irish, he missed much of his third season with an infection, before Irish were liquidated due to financial difficulties in 2023. A Lisfranc injury then put a halt to a solid start at new club Harlequins.

But the lasting damage caused by those ailments - while significant - paled in comparison to his next injury in 2024, when he suffered a permanent loss of hearing in his left ear.

"I had a training session and then the whistle went and my ear felt a bit funny," Joseph told Sky Sports. "We had a pool session afterwards: I got into the swimming pool, got out, and then I couldn't hear anything out of my left ear.

" My understanding is that it's an autoimmune disease - my body overreacted to something that's gone in my ear and just shut off the nerves to be able to hear.

"I remember thinking it's going to be really hard [to play], because I felt like I couldn't communicate to anyone outside me - everything felt a little bit off.

"I was definitely a little bit worried [about being able to continue playing], but I got through it week by week and then got to a place where I said actually, I can live with this. This is going to be alright."

His resilient attitude has shone through, coming through a second Lisfranc injury and a wrist surgery to score four tries in seven games for Gloucester this season, with his red-hot form earning himself the long-awaited second cap that allowed him to dazzle on the international stage.

That tenacity is something England fans will recognise as a Joseph gene. His older brother, Johnathan, made 54 appearances for his country in an eight-year spell in the side between 2012 and 2020.

"I felt a big sense of relief," Johnathan told Sky Sports of his brother's performance against Japan.

"He had his first cap four years ago, and then hasn't been seen [for England] since.

"[Before the game] It was almost like if he doesn't go well now and if things go badly, it could have been his last chance.

"It was a real sense of relief [to see Will perform like that] because I know he's good enough to be in that England team."

Will has undoubtedly been influenced by the sparkling rugby career of his older brother, but it is also his twin brother, Alex, who provides a source of daily inspiration.

The winger speaks warmly of being motivated by taking care of Alex, who suffers with severe learning difficulties and epilepsy.

While focusing on recovering from his own injuries, Will also had to contend with his twin being temporarily put into an induced coma as a result of uncontrolled seizures.

"Growing up with him, I almost felt like I had to look after him," Will added. "He's a big motivator for me because he's probably not able to do things like most people in this world.

"I want to make him proud. He's a big why for me."

His older brother Johnathan echoed this sentiment, attributing Will's composure in high-stakes situations in part to the skills learned when caring for his twin.

"[Will] is a very humble kid. He's very caring - he puts people before himself.

"He's obviously got a twin brother who's got special needs, so he's always had to take care of him, which sort of transfers over to the bloke he is today.

"[Will] was obviously buzzing after [the Japan game], but he'll be right back down to earth now and he'll be working hard to prepare well for New Zealand, I'm sure."

Starting against the ever-vaunted All Blacks - who will be looking for a reprieve after their damaging 35-28 loss to Wales in Cardiff - will undoubtedly be the most high-calibre challenge of Will's career.

But with his track record of overcoming adversity, you would be daft to bet against the Gloucester man putting on another show-stopping performance.
